result.markdown: --- title: "[Graph.which_loops()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method}" body-classes: doc-api-page doc-py-api-page shift-heading-level-by: 0 toc-depth: 3 page-navigation: false html-table-processing: none --- ::: {.doc-subject} Find edge IDs of self-loops (edges from a node to itself). ::: ::: {.doc-usage-source} Usage [Source](https://github.com/rich-iannone/edgecase/blob/main/python/edgecase/graph.py#L28767-L28831){target="_blank" rel="noopener"} ::: ::: {.doc-signature .doc-Kind.FUNCTION} ```python Graph.which_loops() ``` ::: ::: {.doc-text} ![Which loops](/assets/graphs/which-loops.light.svg){.lightbox fig-alt="Four nodes in a row joined by edges 1, 2, 3, with self-loops 4 and 5 on A and 6 on C in the accent color. The card returns the self-loop edge ids 4, 5, 6." width="100%"} Returns a list of edge IDs for all edges where the source node equals the target node. Self-loops are common in certain network types like state machines, chemical reactions, or social networks (self-mentions). ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [list[int]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : List of edge IDs representing self-loops. Empty if no self-loops exist. ::: ## Technical Notes {.doc-technical-notes} Enumerates every edge whose source and target coincide, in insertion order. Directed and undirected graphs are both supported; a single node can carry multiple self-loops and each such edge appears in the returned list. Self-loops distort several graph statistics (they inflate degree by two rather than one, break certain adjacency-matrix identities, and confuse some spectral bounds), so removing them before analysis is a common preprocessing step: `count_loops()` gives the per-node totals, and `remove_selfloops()` clears them in a single pass. ## Examples {.doc-examples} In a directed graph, a self-loop is any edge whose source and target are the same node: ::: {#3e150321 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec g = ec.Graph(directed=True) g.add_node(label="Alice") g.add_node(label="Bob") g.add_node(label="Carol") g.add_edge(source="Alice", target="Bob") g.add_edge(source="Alice", target="Alice") # Self-loop g.add_edge(source="Bob", target="Carol") g.add_edge(source="Carol", target="Carol") # Self-loop # Returns 2 (Alice->Alice and Carol->Carol) len(g.which_loops()) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` 2 ``` ::: ::: In a state machine, self-loops naturally represent states that can transition back to themselves, like a "wait" or "retry" state: ::: {#0d71cec8 .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} fsm = ( ec.Graph(directed=True) .add_node(label="Idle") .add_node(label="Processing") .add_node(label="Complete") .add_edge(source="Idle", target="Processing") .add_edge(source="Processing", target="Processing") # Wait state .add_edge(source="Processing", target="Complete") .add_edge(source="Complete", target="Idle") ) # Returns 1 (the Processing -> Processing wait state) len(fsm.which_loops()) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ``` 1 ``` ::: :::
